title: Q&A: Why are UK energy bills so high – and how could they be lowered? - Carbon Brief
gist: UK household energy bills hit a three-year high (cap £1,723, forecast around +25% in January 2027) mainly because gas drives wholesale prices; Carbon Brief and Nesta find wholesale costs explain more than 80% of the rise since 2020, while network investment is the second driver. The piece argues slowing the clean-power push would not cut bills and that electrification and shifting policy costs off electricity are the main levers.

insights.claim: The UK household price cap hit £1,723 a year in October 2026, up 47% in real terms since October 2020, and is forecast to rise around 25% in January 2027, pushing annual bills towards £2,200.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A further sharp step in UK energy costs is nearly locked in for early 2027, a political and inflation pressure point.
insights.locator: What is driving high energy bills?

insights.claim: Gas prices driven by the Iran war and the Hormuz crisis are the main reason for the October 2026 cap rise, and wholesale costs, tied to gas via marginal pricing, are 44% of the cap.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: UK electricity bills stay hostage to gas prices until marginal pricing is weakened.
insights.locator: Wholesale costs for electricity and gas make up 44%

insights.claim: Nesta analysis shows a surge in wholesale costs from expensive gas is responsible for more than 80% of the rise in dual-fuel household energy bills since 2020, contrary to widespread media and political narratives.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Policy costs and renewables are not the main cause of high bills; counters narratives used to argue for dropping climate goals.
insights.locator: Indeed, Nesta analysis recently published

insights.claim: Of the current cap, network charges make up 24%, operating costs 17% and policy costs only 7%.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Removing policy costs alone has a limited ceiling on bill reductions.
insights.locator: Network charges make up a further 24%

insights.claim: Ofgem approved £29bn of upfront investment in gas and electricity grids at end-2025 as part of up to about £90bn to 2031, and network charges are expected to rise about 50% from £222 to £330 a year for a typical household between 2025 and 2030.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Network operators are the structural winners of a rising regulated asset base while bills rise.
insights.locator: At the end of 2025, energy regulator Ofgem approved

insights.claim: Much of the network cost rise reflects updating ageing infrastructure after decades of under-investment: Ofgem says about three-fifths of the £108 per household rise to 2030 is business-as-usual maintenance and only £30 is for expanding electricity transmission, and ENA says up to 80% of electricity grid investment maintains existing assets.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Grid spending is mainly replacement, not a renewables-driven cost.
insights.locator: Ofgem says some three-fifths

insights.claim: Constraint costs from switching off windfarms and turning on gas plants amount to only £35, or 4%, of typical annual electricity bills, partly reflecting the 2010s 'connect and manage' decision to postpone network investment.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Constraint costs are a small share today but grow if grid build lags generation.
insights.locator: These costs sit within network balancing charges

insights.claim: The National Energy System Operator projects balancing costs could rise from £2bn to £8bn by 2030 if the grid faces delays, though its central projection is £3-4bn.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Grid delays are the key risk scenario for balancing-cost inflation and curtailment of wind.
insights.locator: Projections from the National Energy System Operator

insights.claim: Unpaid-bill 'bad debt' recovered via charges on all households adds about £60 to typical bills, up about £40 since 2020, and Energy UK says rising debt could add another £10-15 by next year.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Bad debt is an increasingly visible bill component and a target for shifting to taxation.
insights.locator: Finally, following years of elevated energy bills

insights.claim: At the 2025 budget the government closed the ECO efficiency scheme and moved 75% of the legacy renewables obligation into general taxation, expected to save a typical household £134 a year.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Policy-cost shifting to the Treasury has precedent and is the template for further steps.
insights.locator: At the 2025 budget

insights.claim: Prime minister Andy Burnham announced removal of VAT from electricity bills for six months from 1 October, cutting bills by around £45.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Temporary measure; watch for extension or permanence decisions.
insights.locator: new prime minister Andy Burnham announced in July

insights.claim: UKERC's Richard Carmichael says the impact of reduced policy costs and VAT has been 'masked' by rising wholesale energy prices.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Gas prices overwhelm marginal policy relief.
insights.locator: Speaking to Carbon Brief, Dr Richard Carmichael

insights.claim: Nesta research suggests UK electricity bills are rising much more slowly than gas this year despite the Hormuz crisis due to clean power expansion, an early sign of electricity prices 'decoupling' from gas.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Evidence that the UK's growing renewables share is starting to dampen gas pass-through.
insights.locator: Nesta research suggests that electricity bills

insights.claim: Analysts told Carbon Brief the April reforms intended to break the link between gas and electricity prices are likely to have only a modest impact, though the link will weaken as more wind and solar is built.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Don't expect near-term relief from market-design reform.
insights.locator: In April, the government announced reforms

insights.claim: Record wind and solar output has let the UK avoid roughly £5.9bn of gas imports since the start of the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Quantifies the energy-security value of renewables during the gas spike.
insights.locator: Since the start of the Iran war

insights.claim: Windfarms cut wholesale power prices by around a third in 2025 through the merit-order effect, according to ECIU, and UCL research finds UK wind cut consumer costs by £104bn over 2010-2023, net of subsidies.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Wind's merit-order effect lowers wholesale prices, undercutting cost-of-subsidy narratives.
insights.locator: In addition to directly displacing gas

insights.claim: More than 120 trade bodies, businesses and charities called for 'hidden taxes' such as the Sizewell C levy, warm home discount and legacy feed-in tariffs to be moved onto general taxation, which they say would raise the total average domestic bill reduction under this government to as much as £250 a year.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Pre-budget pressure points to further policy-cost transfers that would raise fiscal costs.
insights.locator: A September letter to the government

insights.claim: Energy consultant Kate Mulvany says moving policy costs and bad debt into general taxation is 'in all likelihood the fastest route' to reducing bills, but the Treasury has resisted because the money must come from elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Fastest bill relief is a fiscal choice, with a direct budget implication.
insights.locator: Speaking to Carbon Brief, energy consultant Kate Mulvany

insights.claim: A parliamentary Energy Security and Net Zero Committee report calls for moving policy costs from electricity onto gas bills to reduce the 'spark gap'; the ratio of electricity to gas prices was 4.3 in April 2026, has dropped to 3.3 under the latest cap and could fall to 3.0 in January 2027.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
entities: Energy Security and Net Zero Committee
insights.so_what: A lower spark gap improves the running economics of heat pumps and EVs versus gas and petrol.
insights.locator: This is because it would reduce the 'spark gap'

insights.claim: Aurora's Ashutosh Padelkar points to flexibility and dynamic line ratings, where cables can be overloaded for short periods, as ways to improve network efficiency and cut costs.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Flexibility and grid optimisation are the cheapest levers to limit network cost growth.
insights.locator: Ashutosh Padelkar, research lead at Aurora

insights.claim: Nesta says removing standing charges from gas bills would save typical households £27 a year and help encourage the shift to heat pumps and EVs, and Burnham has asked ministers to develop a plan to do so.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Policy under consideration that would change gas supplier revenue structure.
insights.locator: Ahead of the budget, Burnham has asked ministers

insights.claim: Common Wealth and Stonehaven with Greenpeace propose putting gas-fired power stations into a strategic reserve to more completely break the link between gas and power prices.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A radical option that would reshape gas-plant revenues.
insights.locator: Finally, separate proposals from thinktank Common Wealth

insights.claim: Targeted relief proposals such as social tariffs and rising block tariffs carry drawbacks: cliff-edge exclusion for social tariffs and a risk that rising block tariffs discourage electrification.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Design trade-offs mean targeted relief is hard to deliver cleanly.
insights.locator: Another option is to introduce a 'social tariff'

insights.claim: The IFS says continuing to push rapid decarbonisation 'risks increasing costs', based on 2024 NESO modelling that relying on more gas in 2030 could be slightly cheaper, but its deputy research director notes gas prices have risen significantly since, favouring renewables, while capital costs have also risen.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The cost case for slowing the transition depends on stale gas-price assumptions.
insights.locator: For example, a September 2026 report

insights.claim: The Tony Blair Institute argues for an objective of 'cheaper power by 2030' rather than 'clean power 2030', though its latest report focuses on flexibility, grid optimisation and electrification rather than slower renewables, perhaps implicitly acknowledging nuclear and CCS are not cheap.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Think tank positioning moves toward electrification as consensus ground.
insights.locator: Another prominent

insights.claim: The Conservative party opposes clean power 2030, wants all UK climate targets scrapped, and backed an Onward report claiming 'over £320bn' of savings from 'cheap power'; Carbon Brief's factcheck found it relied on questionable assumptions, including that gas and nuclear would be cheap.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Cheap-power alternative claims rest on optimistic gas and nuclear cost inputs.
insights.locator: Perhaps the strongest push to abandon

insights.claim: RWE UK's Tom Glover said the Onward report was a useful scenario presented as a plan, built on 'a stack of optimistic inputs'.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Industry voices doubt the case for gas-heavy scenarios.
insights.quote: There’s a difference between a useful scenario and a plan you’d build a system around.
insights.locator: Tom Glover

insights.claim: Following the start of the Iran war, UK wholesale gas prices, already roughly three times higher than before the Ukraine crisis, have more than doubled again, and RenewableUK counts this as the ninth gas-price spike of the past decade.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Gas-price volatility is frequent, making gas-heavy pathways riskier.
insights.locator: Following the start of the Iran war

insights.claim: ECIU estimates the total cost to the UK economy of higher energy prices after Russia's invasion of Ukraine at £183bn over four years.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Quantifies the macro cost of gas exposure.
insights.locator: (The total cost to the UK economy

insights.claim: RenewableUK argues the 2015 decision to 'cut the green crap' added £22bn to bills by leaving the UK more exposed to volatile fossil-fuel prices.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Historical precedent: slowing renewables increased fossil-price exposure and consumer costs.
insights.locator: He points to the then-Conservative government decision

insights.claim: LCP Delta analysis suggests the UK will reach only 83% clean power by 2030, with the 95% target unlikely before 2035, and the government has said it will not contract more clean power toward the 2030 target unless it lowers bills.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Clean power 2030 is likely to be missed, and further procurement is conditional on cost.
insights.locator: Indeed, recent analysis by consultancy LCP Delta

insights.claim: Electrification spreads fixed network upgrade costs across a larger base of demand, and replacing three parallel energy systems for gas, electricity and petrol with one electric system reduces consumer costs over time, according to SSE.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Higher electric demand lowers per-unit network charges, supporting utility and grid growth cases.
insights.locator: If the UK largely electrifies its economy

insights.claim: Electric cars are currently up to nine times cheaper to run than petrol cars in the UK, according to Carbon Brief analysis.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Running-cost gap supports EV adoption despite high power prices.
insights.locator: Indeed, electric cars are currently up to nine times cheaper

insights.claim: The Climate Change Committee says faster electrification would cut UK household bills today, even including the higher upfront costs of heat pumps, and the government's £13bn 'warm homes plan' claims bill cuts of up to £600 a year through efficiency, heat pumps, solar and batteries.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Policy tailwind for heat pumps, solar and batteries demand.
insights.locator: A recent CCC report

insights.claim: Energy UK's conference delegates ranked electrification and affordability as the top two energy priorities, and even the Conservatives argue the UK must electrify its economy.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Electrification enjoys cross-party support.
insights.locator: At the Energy UK conference in October
